---
order: 7
unit: help
title: When something goes wrong
summary: "Everyone has something go wrong online sometimes: a mean message, a scary picture, a trick, or a mistake of their own. A plan helps: stop and don't reply, keep it (don't delete it), tell a trusted adult, then block and report. Telling early is how things get fixed, and you are not in trouble for asking for help, even if you made a mistake."
language: science
shape: 5e
explainDiagram:
  ref: diagrams.mmd#plan
  alt: "A flowchart of the plan. Something online upsets or worries you. Stop: don't reply. Keep it: don't delete it. Tell a trusted adult. Block and report, together. Get support and look after yourself. A side note: made a mistake yourself? Tell anyway, it can be fixed; it joins the plan at Tell a trusted adult."
  caption: "When something goes wrong"
hook: "Zara gets a nasty message from an account she doesn't know. Her first idea is to delete it and never tell anyone. What might happen if she does?"
---
Zara, Ollie and everything that happens to them are made up. Nobody will ask what has happened to you.

## Engage: delete and forget?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a guess: deleting and staying quiet feels safest, but it leaves Zara alone with it and removes what an adult needs to help."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Zara deletes the nasty message and tells nobody. What is most likely?"
  options: ["It may keep happening, and nobody can help because nobody knows", "It stops, because she deleted it", "The sender gets in trouble automatically"]
  actual: "It may keep happening. Deleting removes what an adult could use to help, and staying quiet means Zara deals with it alone."
```

## Explore: what would help?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting first moves shows that the helpful ones keep things calm and bring in help."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Zara got a nasty message. Does each move help, or make things harder?"
  options: ["Helps", "Makes it harder"]
  items:
    - ["Not replying", "Helps", "A reply can keep it going, and that may be what the sender wants."]
    - ["Taking a screenshot or noting the username, then telling her dad", "Helps", "An adult can help more when they can see what happened."]
    - ["Sending something nasty back", "Makes it harder", "It can make things worse, and it puts Zara in the wrong too."]
    - ["Deleting it and pretending it didn't happen", "Makes it harder", "Nobody can help, and the evidence is gone."]
    - ["Blocking the account and reporting it, with her dad", "Helps", "Blocking stops more messages; reporting tells the app."]
    - ["Talking to a friend and to her teacher about how she feels", "Helps", "Feeling upset is normal. Talking helps."]
```

Was your guess right? The moves that help keep things calm and **bring in help**.

## Explain: the plan

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "The plan as a diagram. The planted mistake is believing that telling gets you in trouble."
diagram:
  ref: diagrams.mmd#plan
  alt: "A flowchart of the plan. Something online upsets or worries you. Stop: don't reply. Keep it: don't delete it. Tell a trusted adult. Block and report, together. Get support and look after yourself. A side note: made a mistake yourself? Tell anyway, it can be fixed; it joins the plan at Tell a trusted adult."
  caption: "When something goes wrong"
  role: explain
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#ollie"
      text: "Ollie made a mistake. Click the line where his thinking first goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: tell-means-trouble
      explain: "Line 3: Ollie thinks telling will get him in trouble, so he hides it. Telling early is how things get fixed. Adults would much rather know, and an account can often be got back if someone acts quickly."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why does the plan say keep it, not delete it?"
      options: ["So a trusted adult can see what happened and help report it", "So you can read it again later", "So you can send it to friends", "Because deleting is against the rules"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Reading it again usually makes you feel worse. You can ask an adult to keep it for you.", "Sending it on spreads it.", "It's not a rule. It's about getting help."]
      explain: "A screenshot or the username helps an adult help you, and helps an app act on a report."
```

When something online upsets or worries you, you don't have to work it out alone:

1. **Stop.** Don't reply.
2. **Keep it.** Don't delete it. A screenshot or the username helps an adult help you. (If it's a picture that shouldn't be shared, such as someone without clothes on, don't save it or send it on: just tell an adult straight away.)
3. **Tell a trusted adult.** A parent or carer, a teacher, the school counsellor.
4. **Block and report,** with the adult. Apps have a report button; the adult knows other places to report too.
5. **Look after yourself.** Feeling upset is normal. Do something you enjoy, and keep talking.

**Made a mistake yourself?** Tell anyway. Everyone makes mistakes online, and most can be fixed, more easily if you tell early. You can also call **Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800**, free, any time.

```code diagrams.mmd#plan
flowchart TD
  A[Something upsets or worries you] --> B[Stop: don't reply]
  B --> C[Keep it: don't delete]
  C --> D[Tell a trusted adult]
  D --> E[Block and report, together]
  E --> F[Get support, look after yourself]
  M[Made a mistake? Tell anyway] --> D
  class D new
```

## Elaborate: which step next?

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Years 7 and 8: the same plan in harder situations, choosing the next step."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Match each situation to the step that comes next in the plan."
  pairs:
    - ["Someone keeps messaging Kai after he asked them to stop. He's already told his mum.", "Block and report, together"]
    - ["Mei sees a fake account using her name and photo. She wants to delete everything she has ever posted.", "Keep it: don't delete"]
    - ["Ari shared a friend's private message by mistake and feels awful.", "Tell a trusted adult"]
    - ["A message makes Priya feel scared. Her first thought is to write back angrily.", "Stop: don't reply"]
```

## Evaluate: your trusted adults

```step
stage: info
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Zara's trusted adult isn't around. What could she do?"
      options: ["Tell another trusted adult, such as a teacher or the school counsellor, or call Kids Helpline", "Wait until she forgets about it", "Reply to the sender to sort it out herself", "Post about it so everyone knows"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It may keep happening, and she's alone with it.", "Replying can keep it going.", "That makes the audience bigger."]
      explain: "Most people have more than one trusted adult, and Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800) is free, any time."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I know the plan: stop, keep it, tell a trusted adult, block and report, look after myself." }
```

**A private think** (just for you): who are your trusted adults? Is there one at home and one at school?

```teacher
summary: "Students predict what happens when a problem is deleted and kept
  secret, sort first moves into helps and makes it harder, and learn a five-step
  plan as a diagram: stop, keep it, tell a trusted adult, block and report, look
  after yourself, with 'made a mistake? tell anyway'. Typical width (Years 7 and
  8): choose the next step in harder situations."
time: 40
timing: Engage and Explore 10 min · Explain 12 min · Elaborate 8 min · Evaluate 10 min
goals:
  - I can say the plan for when something goes wrong online.
  - I can explain why keeping it and telling helps more than deleting.
  - I can explain why telling helps even if I made a mistake.
struggle: "Students believe telling means losing their device or getting in
  trouble. Name that worry out loud as common, and say what adults actually do:
  help."
before: >
  **⚑ Wellbeing review:** this is the course's key lesson for help-seeking. Read
  it with the school's wellbeing lead and child-protection contact before
  teaching. Agree: who students should tell at school, the school's reporting
  process, and how the school responds when a student tells (so the lesson's
  promise that telling helps is true here). One line tells students not to save
  or forward a picture that shouldn't be shared (for example a nude image) and
  to tell an adult straight away; check the wording with the wellbeing lead,
  especially for Years 5 and 6.


  **If a student discloses something:** this lesson invites help-seeking, so a
  disclosure is possible. Follow the school's child-protection procedure.
  Listen, don't probe, don't promise to keep it secret (say you may need to tell
  someone whose job is to help), and pass it on as the procedure says. Thank
  them for telling.


  **Ground rules:** Zara, Ollie, Kai, Mei, Ari and Priya are made up. Never ask
  what has happened to students or people they know, and don't ask for examples.
  Avoid suggesting that devices will be taken away. The closing think is
  private.


  **Support:** the school's wellbeing team; Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800,
  kidshelpline.com.au (free, for young people; checked 26 Oct 2026, check it is
  current); the eSafety Commissioner's reporting pages at esafety.gov.au/report
  (checked 26 Oct 2026) and its pages for kids at esafety.gov.au/kids. No laws
  are stated; eSafety explains what can be reported and how.


  The diagram is a Mermaid flowchart (lesson.md › diagrams.mmd#plan). Years 5
  and 6: give the link with `?width=minimum`.
running:
  - "Engage: ask why deleting feels like the safe choice."
  - "Explore: ask what the 'helps' moves have in common (calm, and bringing in
    help)."
  - "Explain: walk through the diagram; ask who students could tell at school
    (in general, no names needed)."
  - "Elaborate (Years 7 and 8): ask which situation was hardest to place."
  - "Evaluate: say the school's own reporting route and the Kids Helpline number
    aloud."
stuck:
  - see: A student says telling just gets your phone taken away.
    ask: What would you want an adult to do if you told them?
    fix: Adults would much rather know. Telling early is how things get fixed.
  - see: A student says you should fight back.
    ask: What might the sender want you to do?
    fix: Stop and don't reply. Block and report with an adult instead.
  - see: A student becomes quiet or upset, or starts to describe something real.
    ask: (Privately.) Would you like to talk after class?
    fix: Follow the child-protection procedure; involve the wellbeing team.
stretch: Make a poster of the plan for a younger class, in your own words.
support: The diagram printed on a card, with the school's own reporting route added.
leads: >
  Next: our class agreement. The class writes how it will treat each other
  online.


  Links: AI in your life › A fake about someone (Years 7 and up; the same plan
  when a fake is shared).
exit:
  q: Name the first three steps of the plan.
  a: Stop (don't reply), keep it (don't delete), tell a trusted adult.
explain: >
  When something online upsets or worries you: **stop** (don't reply), **keep
  it** (don't delete), **tell a trusted adult**, **block and report** together,
  and **look after yourself**.


  Made a mistake yourself? **Tell anyway.** Most things can be fixed, more
  easily if you tell early.


  Kids Helpline: **1800 55 1800**, free, any time.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Why might someone not tell an adult when something goes wrong online? What
      would make it easier?
    prompts:
      - Think about Ollie and Zara, not yourself.
      - What could an adult say or do that would make telling easier?
    notes: "Common reasons: fear of trouble, of losing a device, of making it worse,
      embarrassment. Use the answers to say what the school actually does when a
      student tells. Keep it general."
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: activity
      title: Our school's version
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Look at the plan. Who at our school could you tell? Where is the report
        button in an app? Add the school's own route to the plan.
      notes: Fill in the school's process (the wellbeing team, a form, a teacher). No
        student names a person they would tell out loud unless they want to.
    - at: end
      kind: info
      title: Where to get help
      do: >
        A trusted adult at home or school. The school's wellbeing team. Kids
        Helpline: 1800 55 1800, free, any time. eSafety Commissioner:
        esafety.gov.au
      notes: Leave this slide up at the end. Check the Kids Helpline number is
        current.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Keep it or delete it?
      type: question
      q: "Someone sends Zara a mean message. Which step comes right after 'Stop: don't
        reply'?"
      options:
        - "Keep it: don't delete"
        - Block the account
        - Send it to friends
      answer: 0
      explain: Keep it first, so a trusted adult can see what happened. Then tell,
        then block and report together.
```

# Ollie's thinking for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the line, nothing runs.

# region: ollie
Ollie clicks a link in a game chat that promised free coins.
His game account starts sending strange messages to his friends.
He thinks: if I tell anyone, I'll get in trouble, so I'll just hide it.
He says nothing, and a week later he can't get into the account at all.
# endregion
